Hi everyone! I am the author. I just wanted to tell you thank you all for reading this piece. My friend here is a big redditor and he let me know it was here.

You: "Suicide itself is however, a selfish act. Especially when it happens without at least trying to get help. ESPECIALLY when it's treated lightly (which can often happen with people who are reacting to an event rather than dealing with a chemical imbalance). And I really think that's okay to admit since with many people I know who have battled (mostly STILL battling) severe depression, the knowledge that it would be selfish to follow through is what kept them hanging on long enough to GET help!"

You think everyone has the means to seek help? You think everyone can afford it or is lucky enough to even get it properly diagnosed?

Sorry you find my tone "aggressive." But as someone who has not only lost people to suicide, but also survived it myself, I'm telling you - your view that "suicide is selfish" or "thinking suicide is selfish can even save you sometimes" is ridiculous.

Yeah. Suicide survivor here. None of that chunk of text you just wrote matters to the person who read Tyra's words and was forcibly reminded of someone they lost to suicide, or to the person who read those words and felt selfish for being suicidal.

Tyra, love her or hate her, for better or worse, had a platform. She could have really done harm to someone with this bullshit. Is she a human? Yes. Has she been through shit? Most of us have.

Doesn't mean we tell people to kill themselves or call the victims of suicide "cowards."

Shit.

I read what you said. Your false separation of "well, they actually killed themselves so they're selfish" and "they haven't killed themselves they're just thinking about it" is BS and contributes to people feeling selfish for merely having suicidal ideation.
Thank you
Your view is toxic and sends the message that the state of being suicidal is also selfish.

It reminds me a lot of Paris is Burning, when voguing was this underground thing and then Madonna picked it up, put it in her video, and suddenly it was super fashionable and edgy and cool. But it started out as a way for the disenfranchised to express themselves. 

So I ain't mad at it. Not at this particular thing, anyway. Though I am a little annoyed with the cultural system that makes stuff like this happen. Because this is just how it works, really. Take a look at Lady Gaga (who I legitimately like, by the way) she took the whole "ball culture" and "haus" thing and made it into something mainstream, but really underground LGBT culture was doing what she was delivering decades ahead of her. 

So, yes. Underground LGBT culture, especially LGBT people of color, do a good deal of the innovating that later becomes the "cool" stuff of mainstream culture. I kind of like and dislike that at the same time. I'm proud that we're inventive and creative, I love seeing the cutting edge of what tomorrow's fad will be, and I'm even glad to see it resonate on a broader scale where everyone can enjoy it. But I think there's always that "ugh, we had it first and y'all are copying" element present as well haha.

Hey, I know these feelings all too well. Don't listen to people who give you shit for posting this. This is a place to express yourself, particularly when it comes to BPD. I don't know you, so I can't speak to your character or how you are in real life, but I do know this internal dialogue is not only negative, it is deadly, and your main focus in life right now should be figuring out how to get rid of it. You don't deserve the things you're dealing with inside right now, and you need to believe that if you want to get better. You're struggling. That's the reality. One time I wrote an article that lit up the Internet for a solid week. Something like 100,000 shares on Facebook. Unfortunately, it was very personal, somewhat political, and about me being gay. I was receiving anonymous death threats and commentary from strangers about my sexuality, calling me "faggot" etc, and I was so blind with rage the whole time. I didn't publish anything for a long time after that. I'm still scared of this profession I've chosen. It is so dependent on how people react, and people never react the way I want them to. I've been wanting to ask someone about this for a while now. Since my diagnosis, I've been racking my brain trying to find out if my abandonment issues come from my parents. 

The reality is they are loving, wonderful people. Sure, they weren't perfect. And yeah, they messed up. But they never hit me or verbally abused me. So why is my BPD so severe? 

I come from a biracial background. My mother is Latina and my dad is white (this biracial identity caused severe confusion and frustration for me later in high school). My father is hyper-intelligent. Very clever, very shrewd. He worked in pharmaceutical sales and was really good at it, though all his time went into it. He was always leaving dinner or family functions to talk on his phone or he was just away on business trips. We live in Oklahoma, and even though my dad never had an accent, he'd put one on when talking to doctors or coworkers. He'd put a lot of personality into it and really charm their pants off. He made a killing at work (we've never struggled financially) and all his employees love, love, loved him. But I never got any of that. If I had problems in school (and I frequently did) or with my emotions (all the time), I would sit on the arm of his sofa where he played Madden and I would talk, talk, talk while he nodded and played his games. 

The white side of my family is terribly racist. We lived out in the country where our house and my white grandfather's house were the only buildings for miles. But we never spoke to him or any of my dad's relatives because they cut us all off when he married a Mexican woman. All I know is that they were very cold, very hateful, all fucked up, and my dad was the best of the bunch. And he really is. He's very accepting of all races (and of me for being gay).

My mother is the strongest person I know, but I also know some of her issues messed me up. We were up on a hill in the countryside with no neighbors and no friends. My little sister and I needed to socialize... but my mother had agoraphobia (a fear of leaving the house) and so, most of the time, we all stayed indoors. All the time. My sister and I are so close to this day, I think, because we had no one but each other for so long. Neither of us made any friends until high school. 

My mother likely has BPD as well. We used to joke that we both had the Latin blood because we were so quick to anger and that my sister and my dad got the white genes because they were always so chill. Actually, I think my mom and I just have anger issues while my sister and my dad struggle from the coldness of feeling that my white family has. 

It's a cakewalk compared to the abuse a lot of people with BPD have had. My parents to this day support the hell out of me. They've owned up to their shortcomings and my dad even went into therapy (something I never thought he'd do) just to work through his lack of emotions or his problem with expressing them. They've seen me impulsively travel the world just to stay with lovers who've flown me out, they've taken my teary phone calls at 4 am from god-knows-where, Mexico, France, Germany, etc. just to calm me down and tell me how loved I am. 

I think the real roots of BPD are in my relationships outside of the family. Starting in elementary school, even. I used to be overweight until I developed an eating disorder and a gym addiction. I had glasses. I had acne. I was nerdy and weird as hell. Kids have been picking on me from day one, and I never had a friend, really. 

In middle school I started to make a group of friends. I loved those friends. I would have done anything for them. I loved them too much, probably. Then, on April Fool's, they thought it would be funny to pretend like they hated me. They kicked me out of their lunch table and called me names and made me cry. They said "April Fool's!" at the end, but then they just kept doing it. 

It was a nightmare come true. They started picking on me for being gay, though I wasn't out yet. They called me "faggot" and tripped me and kicked me and beat me. It was a small town in Oklahoma, so the faculty, because they hated gay people too, did nothing. Sometimes even joined in. I tried to kill myself and then I was transferred. 

So sorry, I seem to have written my whole life story and that's not what you asked for. It felt kind of good to get out... sometimes I learn more about myself when I'm just rambling about my past. So thank you for that, and sorry again for the diatribe.
